race.office: Governor of Alaska (open seat; Gov. Mike Dunleavy term-limited)

nominee.t: Advanced (4th overall, 3rd among the four who advanced). Aug. 18, 2026 top-four nonpartisan primary (17 candidates, 164,303 votes): Kreiss-Tomkins 37,006 (22.5%); Begich 34,172 (20.8%, withdrew); Wilson 16,468 (10.0%); Bronson 13,364 (8.1%); Taylor 11,928 (7.3%); Bishop 11,527 (7.0%, withdrew). Running mate: Josh Church, a financial professional.

ballot.t: Four-candidate ranked-choice general ballot (Nov. 3, 2026): Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins (D) / Zac Johnson; Bernadette Wilson (R) / Mike Shower; Dave Bronson (R) / Josh Church; Treg Taylor (R) / Candice English. Tom Begich (D, 2nd) withdrew Aug. 28 and endorsed Kreiss-Tomkins; Click Bishop (R, 6th) also withdrew, which let Taylor (5th) advance. The Division of Elections' candidate list was updated after 11 p.m. Sept. 4 to show Taylor with English as running mate. First general ballots mailed starting Sept. 18.

oneliner.t: Republican former one-term mayor of Anchorage (2021–2024), retired Air Force lieutenant colonel and airline pilot, and briefly Dunleavy's appointed manager of Ted Stevens Anchorage International Airport (Jan.–Aug. 2025).

born.t: June 26, 1958, Superior, Wisconsin (Wikipedia; his pamphlet gives age 68 and birthplace Superior, WI)

upbringing.t: Raised on the south side of Superior, Wisconsin, by parents Bill and Sandy Bronson. As a boy he delivered the Evening Telegram, and he attended Superior High School. He earned a B.S. in agricultural economics at the University of Wisconsin–Madison, then flew B-52 and B-1B bombers on active duty in the Air Force (1981–1990). He later served in the Air Force Reserve and the Alaska Air National Guard, retiring as a lieutenant colonel. He is married to Debra and has two children.

career.role: Commercial airline pilot (Delta; took early retirement during the pandemic)
Maintenance officer and C-130 pilot; retired lieutenant colonel
Airport manager (appointed by Gov. Dunleavy; resigned after under eight months)

platform.t: Proposes a constitutional amendment requiring a dividend under the 1982–2016 formula, which the Beacon estimates would cost about $2B a year beyond 2025 levels; he did not say how to pay for it. By Sept. 2026 he was arguing a full PFD cannot be reached by budget cuts alone.
School choice through a constitutional amendment so funding follows the student; blames poor schools for out-migration.
Aggressive resource development, more land and housing access, lower energy costs, infrastructure, bureaucracy cuts. Calls a proposed LNG tax provision 'a bad idea'.
Calls data centers inevitable because of AI; says they should be properly regulated but not delayed, citing competition with China.
Would not have let HB 78 (defined-benefit pension) become law; says a defined-benefit plan could work only with outside financial management.
Support law enforcement; 'election integrity measures' (no specifics in his statement).

promises.t: Seek a constitutional amendment for a formula-based PFD (1982–2016 formula).
Seek a constitutional amendment so school funding follows the student.
Cut bureaucracy and red tape; build infrastructure; lower energy costs.

claims.claim: Active-duty Air Force pilot 1981–1990 flying B-52 and B-1B bombers; retired lieutenant colonel.

record.t: Wikipedia lists the same service dates (USAF 1981–1990, AFRC 1992–93, Alaska ANG 1993–2005) and retirement as a lieutenant colonel. No DD-214 or Guard record was reviewed.

claims.claim: Former airport manager of Ted Stevens International Airport.

record.t: Dunleavy appointed him in January 2025. He resigned in August 2025, after less than eight months.
Wikipedia documents Alaska Air National Guard service from 1993 but gives no arrival date; 35 years would mean about 1991.

claims.claim: As mayor he secured funding for the Don Young Port of Alaska and pay raises for Anchorage police.

record.t: Port funding sources and APD contract records were not retrieved.

claims.claim: A full PFD cannot be reached through budget cuts, even if every state worker were fired.

record.t: The Beacon puts the cost of the old formula at about $2B a year above 2025 levels. The state's total payroll was not retrieved, so the comparison could not be checked.

said.t: His administration's records request said the mayor was 'not questioning the results of the election.'

did.t: The same request offered to pay for a 'forensic audit of election technology', citing an observer complaint that a Dominion technician inserted a USB drive. The Anchorage Election Commission had already called the problems 'fairly minor' and unlikely to change any outcome. Whether the audit happened is not reported.

said.t: Conceded the 2024 runoff and committed to 'a smooth transition'.

did.t: His term ended July 1, 2024, when Suzanne LaFrance succeeded him.

promises_prev.promise: No mask or vaccine mandates — treat them as personal choice (2021 mayoral stance)

evidence.t: As mayor he declined to impose mask or vaccine requirements, calling them a personal choice.

complicating.t: His specific 2021 campaign platform documents were not retrieved; this is recorded from his documented stance in office.

promises_prev.promise: Address homelessness after closing the Sullivan Arena mass shelter (2023 plan for a new 200-bed shelter/navigation center)

evidence.t: He closed the Sullivan Arena shelter in May 2023. The Assembly rejected his plan for a 200-bed shelter, which had started construction without secured funding or an operating plan.

complicating.t: He also suggested sending homeless residents to Los Angeles and other cities. The detailed timeline and dollar figures were not retrieved.

promises_prev.promise: Re-election (2024) on a record including port funding, police raises and the gas shortage response

evidence.t: He lost the May 14, 2024 runoff to LaFrance (about 46%–54%) and conceded May 23, citing those items as accomplishments.

complicating.t: The accomplishments are his own characterization; not independently verified.

entries.t: No mask or vaccine mandates; said he would not be vaccinated and called the vaccine 'experimental'.
Constitutional amendment for the 1982–2016 formula dividend.
Says a full PFD cannot be reached through cuts alone (aimed at Wilson).
Proposed 2024 operating budget cutting about $2.4M from roughly $600M.
With Taylor, urges voters to rank 'one, two, three, just not JKT'; warns GOP infighting could cost Republicans the race.

checks.legal: CourtListener was blocked. Alaska CourtView was not searched directly. Searched news (Alaska Beacon, Alaska Public Media, ADN, KTUU, Sol de Medianoche) and the APOC final order (via DocumentCloud). Found: the 2021 APOC campaign-finance penalty and the Demboski lawsuit (settled 2024). No criminal matters found. Anchorage Board of Ethics records were not searched.
checks.foreign: FARA was blocked. No foreign ties found in news or his pamphlet.
checks.claims: Campaign site davebronson.com could not be fetched (tool provenance block). As a stand-in, used his candidate-authored Official Election Pamphlet statement (which has almost no checkable figures), his 2024 concession statement, and his forum remarks. No ad scripts were found. Five claims: 2 rated true, 3 unverifiable.
checks.democracy: Never in Congress. Searched news for statements on 2020/2024 presidential results (none found), his 2022 municipal election audit request, and his 2024 concession.

legal.t: Acting on a complaint from opponent Forrest Dunbar's campaign, APOC found that Bronson for Mayor filed inaccurate or incomplete reports in the 2021 race (AS 15.13.040(a)): omitted or understated debts, including a $95,000 debt to Hackney & Hackney disclosed months late, and missing subcontractor detail. APOC also found he did not promptly return over-limit contributions but imposed no penalty for that because of Thompson v. Hebdon. It found aggravating factors and no mitigating ones.
legal.status: Final order Oct. 11, 2021: $38,500 civil penalty (maximum calculated). Payment and any appeal were not found.

legal.t: Amy Demboski, a city manager he appointed and later fired, sued in 2023 alleging she was fired in retaliation for raising concerns about illegal and unethical activities in his administration. The Anchorage Assembly approved a $250,000 settlement on Oct. 8, 2024, after he left office; no court finding or admission of liability was reported.
legal.status: Settled Oct. 8, 2024 ($250,000, paid by the Municipality); no finding or admission

record_extra.t: Defended mask-mandate opponents' use of Holocaust imagery (yellow Stars of David) at an Assembly meeting, at first calling it a 'credit' to Jews. He later retracted the remark and said protesters should use a different symbol.
Ordered water fluoridation halted over reported worker symptoms, then let it resume after learning municipal code requires it.

The large 2024 donors listed are individuals; their employers are given for context only, and these are not corporate contributions. A Sol de Medianoche piece repeats Dunbar-campaign allegations from 2021, but only APOC's final order is recorded. office_years counts the mayoralty only (3); the 2025 airport manager post was an appointed administrative job.
